content: Schizophrenia is a chronic and often disabling psychiatric disorder characterized by a wide range of symptoms. While positive symptoms, such as hallucinations and delusions, typically respond well to antipsychotic medications, the cognitive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia are more challenging to treat. These symptoms, which include deficits in motivation, emotional expression, and cognitive functioning, significantly impair quality of life and social outcomes. Conventional antipsychotics are generally ineffective in addressing these aspects of the illness. Selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (NRIs) are pharmacological agents that increase dopamine and noradrenaline levels in the prefrontal cortex without substantially affecting subcortical dopamine levels. This mechanism makes NRIs a promising candidate for targeting the cognitive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of NRIs, compared to placebo or other control treatments, in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia or related disorders. A comprehensive search of the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group’s Trials Register was conducted, which included databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, BIOSIS, AMED, PubMed, and PsycINFO, as well as clinical trial registries. The search was unrestricted by language, date, document type, or publication status. References from included studies were also reviewed to identify additional relevant trials. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing NRIs to placebo or control treatments in individuals with schizophrenia or related disorders were included. Trials were required to meet predefined selection criteria and provide usable data. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by multiple reviewers. For binary outcomes, risk ratios (RR) were calculated, while mean differences (MD) were used for continuous outcomes. Standardized mean differences (SMD) were derived for cognitive outcomes. All results were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI) using a random-effects model. The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed, and the GRADE approach was employed to summarize the quality of evidence for key outcomes. The search identified 113 records, of which 48 were reviewed in full text. Sixteen trials, involving a total of 919 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Most participants were adults with schizophrenia or related disorders, primarily in inpatient settings, and many appeared to have chronic presentations of the illness. Reboxetine was the NRI used in nine of the trials, while atomoxetine and viloxazine were used in the remaining studies. Fourteen trials compared NRIs to placebo, and two trials compared reboxetine to an active control (citalopram) at different time points (4 weeks and 24 weeks), precluding meta-analysis of these data. One trial was described as open and was deemed to have a high risk of bias for randomization and blinding. Additional risks of bias were identified in three trials for attrition, six for reporting, and two for other sources. The primary outcomes of interest included significant improvement in negative and positive symptoms, global clinical status, cognitive functioning, quality of life, and adverse events such as nausea. All data were derived from short-term follow-up periods. 1. Negative Symptoms: One trial (n = 50) reported significantly greater improvement in negative symptom scores on the PANSS negative subscale for participants receiving NRIs compared to placebo (RR 3.17, 95% CI 1.52 to 6.58). However, the quality of evidence was very low. 2. Positive Symptoms: No data were available for significant improvement in positive symptoms. However, endpoint PANSS positive scores from five trials (n = 294) showed no significant difference between NRIs and placebo (MD −0.16, 95% CI −0.96 to 0.63). The quality of evidence was low. 3. Global Clinical Status: One trial (n = 28) reported no significant difference in clinical global status improvement between NRIs and placebo (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.45 to 2.20). The quality of evidence was very low. 4. Cognitive Functioning: No data were reported for significant improvement in cognitive functioning. Average composite cognitive scores from four trials (n = 180) showed no significant difference between NRIs and placebo (SMD 0.04, 95% CI −0.28 to 0.36). The quality of evidence was low. 5. Quality of Life: Data on significant improvement in quality of life were not reported. However, one trial (n = 114) reported better average endpoint scores on the GQOLI-74 for participants receiving NRIs compared to placebo (MD 9.36, 95% CI 7.89 to 10.83). The quality of evidence was very low. 6. Adverse Events: Rates of all-cause withdrawals did not differ significantly between NRIs and placebo (8 RCTs, n = 401; RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.39). Rates of nausea were also not significantly higher with NRIs (3 RCTs, n = 176; RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.41). The quality of evidence for these outcomes was moderate to low. In conclusion, the findings provide tentative, very low-quality evidence suggesting that NRIs, particularly reboxetine, may have a beneficial effect on the negative symptoms of schizophrenia. However, there is limited evidence to suggest that NRIs have any impact on positive symptoms or cognitive functioning. NRIs appear to be generally well-tolerated, with no significant differences in adverse effects such as nausea compared to placebo. These results are based on short-term data and are of poor quality. Further high-quality research, including large RCTs with longer follow-up periods, is needed to better evaluate the efficacy and safety of NRIs, particularly for negative and cognitive symptoms, as well as to provide more comprehensive reporting of outcomes and adverse events.
